title: What is an API?
subtitle: How client-server communication works, REST, JSON, and why APIs exist
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Web applications need to exchange data with servers — fetch a user's profile, submit a form, get weather data, post a tweet. Without a standard way to do this, every connection would require a custom protocol.
whyItExists.solution: APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) define a contract: here are the URLs you can call, what data to send, and what you'll get back. REST is the most common style — it uses HTTP (the same protocol as loading web pages) and JSON for the data format.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever your app needs data from a server, a third-party service, or another application. Weather data, user accounts, product catalogs, payment processing, maps — all delivered via APIs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When data lives entirely in the browser (localStorage, IndexedDB), no API call needed. When building a simple static page with no dynamic data.

explainModes.beginner: An API is like a waiter in a restaurant. You (the client) tell the waiter (the API) what you want. The waiter goes to the kitchen (the server), gets the food (data), and brings it back to you. You never go into the kitchen — you only talk to the waiter. In web development, you send an HTTP request to an API URL, and the server sends back data (usually JSON).
explainModes.simple: Client → HTTP Request → Server → HTTP Response → Client. REST API: uses URLs as nouns (GET /users, POST /posts), HTTP methods as verbs (GET=read, POST=create, PUT/PATCH=update, DELETE=remove). JSON: the data format — { "name": "Alice", "age": 30 }. Endpoint: one specific URL the API exposes (https://api.example.com/users/42). Base URL: the root all endpoints share. Status code: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
explainModes.standard: REST (Representational State Transfer): architectural style, not a protocol. 6 constraints: stateless, client-server separation, cacheable, uniform interface, layered, code on demand (optional). Stateless: each request contains all information needed — no session on the server. Resources: nouns in URLs (/users, /products). Representations: JSON, XML, or other formats. CRUD → HTTP: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE. Hypermedia (HATEOAS): responses contain links to related actions — rarely used in practice.
explainModes.technical: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: 1.1 = text-based, one request at a time per connection. 2 = binary, multiplexed (many requests over one connection), header compression. 3 = uses QUIC/UDP instead of TCP, lower latency. Content negotiation: Accept header (client preference), Content-Type header (what was actually sent). API versioning: URL path (/v1/users), query param (?version=1), header (Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=1). OpenAPI/Swagger: machine-readable API specification format — tooling generates docs, clients, and mocks from it.
explainModes.deepDive: REST alternatives: GraphQL (single endpoint, client specifies shape of data — no over/under-fetching), gRPC (binary protocol buffers, strongly typed, excellent for microservices, not browser-native), WebSocket (persistent bidirectional connection for real-time), Server-Sent Events (one-way server push). JSON:API, HAL, JSON-LD: standardized JSON response formats that add conventions for relationships, pagination, and linking. The 'REST maturity model' (Richardson): Level 0 (single URL, all via POST), Level 1 (resources), Level 2 (HTTP methods + status codes), Level 3 (HATEOAS). Most production APIs are Level 2.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code indicates that a new resource was successfully created by a POST request?
questions.explanation: 201 Created specifically means a new resource was created as a result of the request. The response body typically contains the new resource. 200 OK is for successful requests that return data. 204 No Content is for successful requests with no body (like DELETE). 202 Accepted means the request was received but processing hasn't completed yet (async operations).

faq.q: What's the difference between an API and a REST API?
faq.a: API (Application Programming Interface) is a general term — it just means an interface for two pieces of software to communicate. REST (Representational State Transfer) is a specific *style* of designing web APIs. A REST API uses HTTP, treats data as resources at URLs, and uses HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) as actions. Most web APIs are REST APIs, but you'll also encounter GraphQL APIs, gRPC services, and WebSocket APIs.

examples: GitHub API — manage repos, issues, PRs programmatically
Stripe API — process payments in your app
OpenWeather API — get weather data by city
